name: Blue Lagoon
who: Milky-blue geothermal lagoon fed by power-plant runoff, day tickets + the members-only Retreat spa/hotel.
why: The venue that put geothermal bathing on the world tourism map; still Iceland's single most-visited attraction.

name: Sky Lagoon
who: Infinity-edge oceanfront lagoon minutes from downtown Reykjavik with a 7-step Skjol ritual (sauna, cold plunge, mist, salt scrub, steam).
why: Design-forward answer to Blue Lagoon's crowds — turf-roofed, basalt-set, built the ritual-circuit format other new lagoons now copy.

name: Forest Lagoon
who: Two geothermal pools set into a spruce forest slope above Akureyri, with swim-up sauna and cold tub.
why: Iceland's lagoon boom reaches the north — same warm-water format, a quieter forest setting, and far fewer crowds.

name: Myvatn Nature Baths
who: Sulphur-rich geothermal lake bath in Iceland's volcanic north, with two natural-steam caves on site.
why: Same mineral-blue water and drive-up day access as Blue Lagoon, at a fraction of the price and the crowd.

name: 7132 Therme (Therme Vals)
who: Peter Zumthor's 1996 quartzite thermal bath carved into an Alpine hillside; day access plus the 7132 Hotel.
why: The reference point for thermal-bath architecture worldwide — every minimalist stone spa since owes it a debt.

name: Aqua Dome
who: Tyrol thermal resort with rooftop infinity pools framed by the Otztal Alps; day spa + hotel.
why: One of the Alps' most photographed thermal skylines — the pools appear to float over the mountains.

name: Therme Bucuresti
who: Europe's largest thermal wellness complex — pools, water park, and Bali- and palm-themed halls near Bucharest.
why: Sheer scale: a whole indoor tropical world of thermal pools, saunas, and rituals under one roof.

name: Takaragawa Onsen
who: Riverside rotenburo (open-air bath) ryokan in the Gunma mountains, mixed-bathing pools along the Takaragawa river; day visits bookable.
why: One of Japan's most famous outdoor onsen settings — vast river-stone pools ringed by forest, unchanged for generations.

name: Sainokawara Rotenburo (Kusatsu Onsen)
who: Large public open-air bath fed by Kusatsu's famously acidic, high-volume hot spring water; walk-in day admission.
why: Kusatsu is one of Japan's three great historic onsen towns, and this rotenburo is its signature public soak.

name: Hakone Yunessun
who: Theme-park-style onsen resort with novelty baths (wine, coffee, sake pools) alongside a traditional Japanese-only bathing area.
why: The onsen-as-entertainment format — playful novelty baths pull a different, younger crowd than classic ryokan bathing.

name: Kinosaki Onsen
who: Willow-lined onsen town with seven public bathhouses (sotoyu); ryokan guests get a free hopping pass, day visitors buy a JPY 1,500 pass.
why: The gold standard for onsen-town culture: strolling between historic bathhouses in yukata is the whole ritual, not just the soak.

name: Peninsula Hot Springs
who: Australia's original geothermal bathing destination — hillside pool amphitheatre, cave pools, and a bathhouse; day and adults-only sessions.
why: Built Australia's hot-springs category from nothing in 2005 and remains its biggest and most complete circuit.

name: Ten Thousand Waves
who: Japanese-style mountain bathhouse above Santa Fe with communal and private outdoor hot tubs, spa, and inn; day access bookable.
why: Introduced Japanese onsen etiquette and design to the American Southwest in 1981 and still defines it.

name: Esalen Institute Hot Springs
who: Cliffside sulfur baths over the Pacific at the retreat that helped invent the modern human-potential movement; public access is a limited nightly 1-3am reservation.
why: The single most storied hot spring in American counterculture history — even with a narrow public window, it belongs.
warning: Public bathing is reservation-only, limited to roughly 1-3am nightly and capped at ~20 guests; daytime access is workshop/lodging guests only.

name: Ojo Caliente Mineral Springs
who: New Mexico resort built around four distinct mineral springs (iron, lithia, soda, arsenic) plus mud pools; day spa and hotel.
why: One of the few sites in the world with four chemically distinct springs in one place, soaked continuously since pre-colonial times.

name: Glen Ivy Hot Springs
who: Southern California day-spa resort famous for its red-clay mud bath, mineral pools, and 19 pools/spas total.
why: SoCal's best-known mud-and-mineral day resort, drawing crowds from LA and San Diego for over a century of operation as a spa.

name: Banff Upper Hot Springs
who: Parks Canada-run mountaintop hot spring pool in Banff National Park, open daily; reopened spring 2026 after a renovation.
why: The find that led to Canada's national-park system in 1885 — soaking with Rockies peaks on every side.

name: Termas Geometricas
who: 17 red-stained wooden pools linked by a raised walkway through a volcanic ravine in Villarrica National Park; open daily year-round.
why: The most architecturally distinct hot spring in South America — a slot canyon reimagined as a bathing circuit.

name: Termas de Puyuhuapi
who: Boat-access-only lodge on a fjord in Chilean Patagonia with floating hot-spring pools; day-trip packages available from Puyuhuapi village.
why: A hot spring reachable only by sea, ringed by temperate rainforest and fjord — remoteness as the whole draw.

name: Pamukkale (Hierapolis Thermal Pools)
who: UNESCO travertine terraces and Cleopatra's Antique Pool (Roman columns underwater); combined site ticket plus a separate pool ticket, reopened after 2026 renovation.
why: A natural wonder that's also a bathing site — 2,000-year-old thermal water over white calcium terraces, still swimmable.

name: Polynesian Spa
who: Lakeside geothermal spa on Lake Rotorua with acidic and alkaline mineral pools in use since the 1880s; day admission.
why: New Zealand's original geothermal bathing institution, in the country's most famous geothermal region.

name: Thermae Bath Spa
who: Britain's only naturally warm mineral spa, with a rooftop pool overlooking Bath Abbey, in the Roman/Georgian spa city; day sessions bookable.
why: The only place in the UK where you can still legally bathe in the water that made Bath a Roman and Georgian spa town.
